gloss: call out; call, summon, name; proclaim; read aloud
summary: קָרָא is to call out with the voice: to call to someone and so summon or invite him, to call on Yahweh, to give or speak a name, to proclaim a day or a message, and to read a book aloud in people's hearing. Its noun מִקְרָא is the calling out itself: a summons that gathers the people (the מִקְרָא קֹדֶשׁ, holy convocation, of each appointed time in Leviticus 23), and the reading aloud of the law (Neh 8:8). Akkadian, Ugaritic and Phoenician share call and invoke, Phoenician and Arabic share read; the Aramaic of Daniel and Ezra and the Peshitta use the same verb for calling, naming and reading. The same spelling also serves a verb of meeting and befalling (לִקְרַאת, to meet), which scripture also writes קרה; its link to calling is not established.

words.summary: The act of calling out, made a noun: the summons that gathers the people, and the reading that calls out the words of a book. Leviticus 23 calls the sabbath and the chief days of the appointed times each a מִקְרָא קֹדֶשׁ, a holy calling-together, which Israel is to proclaim (קָרָא) and on which no work is done.

senses.definition: A calling of the people together: a summoned assembly. A מִקְרָא קֹדֶשׁ, holy convocation, is an assembly called on a holy day, on which no work of labour is done.

evidence.note: The silver trumpets are “for the calling of the congregation (לְמִקְרָא הָעֵדָה)”: when both are blown, all the congregation gathers at the tent of meeting (Num 10:3).
The appointed times of Yahweh, which Israel proclaims as holy convocations: the noun answers to the verb.
“New moon and sabbath, the calling of a convocation (קְרֹא מִקְרָא): I cannot bear iniquity with the solemn assembly (עֲצָרָה).”
The sabbath.
The first day of Unleavened Bread (and its seventh day, Lev 23:8).
The day of Weeks.
The first day of the seventh month, a remembrance of teruah.

words.summary: A verb of meeting: to come upon someone, in friendship or in battle, or of trouble, to befall. Its infinitive with לְ, לִקְרַאת, is “to meet, toward”. Scripture writes the same verb also with ה (קָרָה): the same idiom “lest harm befall him” is spelled with א at Gen 42:4 and with ה at Gen 44:29, “the God of the Hebrews has met with us” with ה at Exo 3:18 and with א at Exo 5:3, and 2Sa 1:6 has both in one phrase. Ugaritic keeps qry “meet” apart from qrʾ “call”. So the evidence points to a third-weak root קרה written here with א; its link to calling is not established.

words.summary: The Peshitta's ܩܪܐ (qrā). Its New Testament keeps the Hebrew uses where it takes up the Old: the voice “calling” in the wilderness, “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord”, “out of Egypt I called my son”, “my name is called over them”; and it is the verb for reading the law and the prophets in the synagogue. In 1Co 15:52 the horn “calls” (תֵּקרֵא) when the dead are raised.

cognates.note: Yehawmilk of Byblos: “I called my Lady Baalat of Byblos and she heard my voice” (KAI 10); Neo-Punic “read the inscription on this stele” (KAI 165); a Punic qrʾ “crier or lector” (CIS i 4883). Phoenician has both the calling and the reading.

cognates.gloss: read, recite; (said to be primary) collect, put together
cognates.note: Lane gives “he read, or recited” a book or scripture, aloud or not, and reports the Arab lexicographers' view that the first sense is “collected together”. Arabic does not use it for calling.
A third-weak root, kept apart from qrʾ “call” in the same glossary: the cognate of the Hebrew verb of meeting (קָרָה, here written קָרָא), not of calling.

doctrine.statement: From the days of Enosh people began to call on the name of Yahweh (Gen 4:26). Abram builds an altar wherever he settles and calls on Yahweh's name (Gen 12:8). On Carmel the test is which God answers the one who calls on his name, and Yahweh answers by fire (1Ki 18:24, 38). Yahweh is near to all who call on him in truth (Psa 145:18); he says “call to me and I will answer you” (Jer 33:3), and “before they call I will answer” (Isa 65:24). Joel says that everyone who calls on the name of Yahweh will be saved, and that among the survivors are those whom Yahweh calls (Jol 3:5): the calling goes both ways. Zephaniah looks to the peoples calling on the name of Yahweh, all of them, to serve him (Zep 3:9). Peter quotes Joel at Pentecost (Act 2:21), and Paul quotes it to say there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is rich to all who call on him (Rom 10:12–13), and asks how they can call on him in whom they have not believed (Rom 10:14). The Peshitta keeps Joel's verb in both places. So those who belong to the Messiah are “all who call on the name of our Lord Jesus the Messiah” (1Co 1:2): the name of Yahweh called on in Joel is the name of Jesus in Paul.

Yahweh calls his people: “I have called you by your name; you are mine” (Isa 43:1); “I, Yahweh, have called you in righteousness” (Isa 42:6); “out of Egypt I called my son” (Hos 11:1), which Matthew reads of Jesus brought back from Egypt (Mat 2:15). To have his name called over a people or a house is to be his: Joab will not take a city lest his own name be called over it (2Sa 12:28), and the peoples will fear Israel when they see that the name of Yahweh is called over them (Deu 28:10). Amos foresees all the nations over whom Yahweh's name is called (Amo 9:12), and James cites it to show that God takes from the nations a people for his name (Act 15:14–17). The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out (Jhn 10:3), and those God marked out beforehand he also called, and justified, and glorified (Rom 8:30).

Yahweh's appointed times are days Israel is to call out: “the appointed times of Yahweh, which you shall proclaim as holy convocations” (Lev 23:2, 4, 37), each a מִקְרָא קֹדֶשׁ on which the people are called together and do no work (Lev 23:3–36). In the fiftieth year, after the shofar has sounded on יוֹם הַכִּפֻּרִים, Israel proclaims liberty in the land (Lev 25:9–10). The calling is also of the word: at Sukkot in the year of release the law is to be read before all Israel in their hearing, men, women, children and the stranger, so that they hear and learn to fear Yahweh (Deu 31:10–12). After the return, Ezra reads the law to the assembly on the first day of the seventh month, distinctly, giving the sense, so that they understand the reading (Neh 8:2–8), and through the seven days of Sukkot he reads in it day by day (Neh 8:18). Isaiah's anointed one is sent to proclaim liberty to captives and to proclaim the year of Yahweh's favour (Isa 61:1–2). Jesus stands up in the synagogue on the sabbath to read, reads this passage, and says, “Today this scripture is fulfilled in your hearing” (Luk 4:16–21).

note: Words left out: קוֹרֵא Kore (BDB s.cy.ac), a Levite's name, for a name entry. BDB's s.cy.aa key total (1355) includes 615 tokens of the spelling לִי “to me”, a spelling-index artifact, so its use count is far too high; the participle tokens are also counted under קֹרֵא (s.cy.ab), whose true uses as “partridge” are only 1Sa 26:20 and Jer 17:11. The niphal tokens are listed under both s.cy.aa and s.cz.aa; the sense split here (named / met) follows the verses. The meeting verb (s.cz.aa, with לִקְרַאת, BDB's s.cz.ab קְרַאת has no tokens of its own) is kept in this entry by its spelling, as asked; the evidence (Gen 42:4 ‖ 44:29, Exo 3:18 ‖ 5:3, 2Sa 1:6, and Ugaritic qry “meet” beside qrʾ “call”) points to a third-weak root קרה. OPEN QUESTION for review: move it to a קרה entry (with קָרָה, מִקְרֶה “chance”, קוֹרָה “beam”?), or keep it here? Also for review: (1) the doctrine items are drafted from the verses only; the second takes Matthew's reading of Hos 11:1 and James's of Amo 9:12 as they stand. (2) The LXX renders מִקְרָא קֹדֶשׁ κλητὴ ἁγία, and Paul greets believers as κλητοῖς ἁγίοις (Rom 1:7; 1Co 1:2; Peshitta קרַיָא וקַדִּישֵא, “called and holy”); the New Testament does not quote Lev 23 there, so this is not entered as evidence; worth the user's judgement. (3) Exo 19:16–19 (God descends, the shofar sounds, the people go out לִקְרַאת הָאֱלֹהִים) and 1Th 4:16–17 (the Lord descends, the trumpet, we go to meet him, εἰς ἀπάντησιν; the Peshitta uses ܐܘܪܥܐ, not ܩܪܐ) share their terms; not entered as doctrine. (4) The “name” senses (qal name, niphal/pual be called) name no cognate: none checked shows naming, so lexicon-support counts the root's cognates against them; the partridge likewise has no cognate. Cognates checked: Lane قرأ pp. 2502–2504 (and قرى p. 2988, the Supplement, nothing for meeting); Oracc qerû and qerītu; Segert's glossary p. 200 read from the Archive.org OCR only (no PDF renderer available to check the page image); Krahmalkov pp. 430–431 from the local text; Anderson–Moser SEM000334. Wiktionary was used only as a lead. Not consulted: DULAT, CAD, Dillmann/Leslau (Ge'ez), Sabaic. Lane also reports قَرْءٌ “menstrual period; time”, not entered.
